title: Welcome
text: Welcome to the Data Science Breakfast Club

title: Lab Charter
text:
“Scientia per communionem” (knowledge through fellowship) emphasises the founding ethos of our lab group: collaboration, learning, and sharing of knowledge for the benefit of all.
Much like the medical firm (now lost to time) the academic lab group is a wonderful, shared community. It brings together like minded individuals on a journey to better themselves and expand their knowledge. It provides a solid core that persists for members as they move between placements, careers or even countries.
Why have a charter? Over time, labs mature and often develop their own scientific “political” leanings. In our experience, this can contribute to the negative interface between science (the method of learning) and academia (the human implementation of that method). Put another way, “successful” labs are often not defined by the quality of their scientific discovery, but by their ability to deluge the market with thematic papers and control the narrative around “their” subject. We aim to redefine what success looks like in medical academia. By building a charter, we can hold ourselves accountable to the standards we have chosen to set. We aim to be an aspirational force, with scientific discovery at its core. This requires a fundamental honesty: that we do not know, are not an authority, and can and will be wrong.

title: Lab Charter
text:
Core Principles

Knowledge can never be owned, only shared[1].
A successful fellow is a successful lab; lift each other up.
Individual differences are to be celebrated and respected. We are united by a passion for acquiring and sharing knowledge.
Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; all opinions are provisional and can be falsified by further experimentation and study.
Be ruthless in experimental planning and design. Never build a study because the data was there and it was convenient.
If it isn’t replicable, it didn’t happen.

title: Ed Palmer
text:
I am a consultant in anaesthesia and intensive care medicine based in London, UK. My research background is in the reuse of routinely collected longitudinal healthcare data for research. My interests are directed towards research goals that may be challenging to meet under traditional frameworks because anticipated effect sizes are very small, that it is too expensive to run a classical trial, or there are concerns over equipoise. My PhD investigated the safe limits—including addressing intrinsic biases—of these resources. This ties with my clinical interest in sepsis, where my research took steps towards a better understanding of “time zero” and the association between physiological trajectories and outcomes in sepsis.
I started this lab group as a way to bring together and support like minded individuals, improve local patient care using data informed methods, and engage with research in a positive way.
The lab group name “The Data Science Breakfast Club” is a loving nod to my long time friend and mentor Prof. Steve Harris, who started a club by the same name more than a decade ago. It was through meeting Steve that my love for this subject florished, and in many respects, this is my attempt at paying it forward.
As a past fellow of the Software Sustainability Institute, I am a strong proponent of open data, reproducible research and free1 and open software. When I am not tinkering with ventilators or R, I try to spend as much time as possible with my wonderful partner and children.

title: Onboarding
text:
Our onboarding process is heavily inspired by Prof. Whittacre’s Lab group. Onboarding aims to:

Complete a minimum example of using git and github
Writing a short member profile
Investing some time in the lab

This process also serves to create a front end directory of lab members, building our community over time.
In order to “onboard”, please complete the following technical steps:

Install git on your local machine
Clone a copy of this website repo and create a new branch
This branch should be identified by your name
Add a profile page in the people folder, and tag yourself with the category of “active lab member”. Please take a look at any of the other profiles for examples.
push your branch to github and submit a pull request.

This will complete the technical aspects of onboarding. You will have learnt through this process, all the vital steps that we will be using for sharing code and completing project peer review. If it feels daunting, please do not worry. We are all here to help you with this process.
Beyond this, new members are expected to:

Read and understand the lab charter.
Come and show us something you are working on.
Contribute your knowledge and experience to others in the lab (as we will do with you.)

We look forward to seeing you in the lab!
